claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength but favorable plasticity and machinability.
The relatively low hardness and strength of this CoCrFeNiTi alloy are governed by modest lattice distortion.
Modest lattice distortion produces insufficient dislocation pinning.
A slight compositional imbalance or tailored annealing can promote local short-range ordering or nanoscale precipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Short-range-ordered regions or nanoscale precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Composition- or annealing-induced ordering or precipitation increases lattice distortion and dislocation barriers.
Increased dislocation pinning from ordering or precipitation raises hardness and yield strength while reducing ductility.
Increasing Cr content in other high-entropy alloys can improve strength and hardness at the expense of ductility.
Similar atomic sizes and a random elemental distribution in nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi produce only modest lattice distortion.
Random elemental distributions in concentrated solid solutions can create inherent chemical inhomogeneity and slip-plane-dependent atomic arrangements.
The baseline CoCrFeNiTi alloy can be produced by conventional casting or thermomechanical processing as a single-phase solid solution.
The baseline CoCrFeNiTi solid solution retains the stated combination of high plasticity and moderate hardness and strength from room temperature to 600 °C.
The modified alloy should exhibit a 10–20% increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy should exhibit less plasticity than the baseline.
The comparison should test baseline and modified samples at 25 °C and 600 °C under an identical strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
The proposed scope excludes processing conditions that form coarse brittle intermetallic phases.
XRD peak shifts or broadening and high-resolution TEM can be used to assess increased lattice distortion, local ordering, or nanoscale precipitates.
Failure to observe increased ordering or lattice distortion and a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention and mediator permit nanoscale precipitate formation, whereas the boundary says the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution. A precipitate-containing state is not strictly single phase, even if coarse brittle intermetallics are absent.
